phonemes.desc: Short close-mid [o], the stressed vowel of the first syllable — Old Irish stress falls always on the first syllable.
Lenited [ɣ], the voiced velar fricative of Spanish 'lago', before the bilabial nasal [m]; the g is softened, never the hard stop of English 'dogma'.
Short final [a], lightly sounded; the name closes open, without a final consonant.

pronunciation.approximation: 'OG-ma' — a short, closed 'o', the g melted toward a soft gargle before the m, stress firmly on the first syllable. The English habit of a hard g, as in 'dogma', is the one sound to avoid.

kin.form: Ogma mac Elathan, 'Ogma son of Elatha', champion of the Túatha Dé Danann

kin.label: Gaulish
kin.form: Ogmios — Lucian's name for the Gaulish Herakles of eloquence, the standard cognate of the Irish name

kin.label: Proto-Celtic
kin.form: *Ogmios, the reconstructed form from which the Irish and Gaulish names descend (LEIA, s.v. Ogma)

kin.label: Epithet

pronunciation.note: Ogma is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Irish form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, and only the capital distinguishes the temple form from the input. The lexicon's traditional gloss is 'the grim one', but the etymology is genuinely unsettled: the standard scholarly line derives the name from Proto-Celtic *Ogmios (attested in Gaulish), with a possible further link to Greek ogmos, 'furrow, swath' — a derivation discussed since Vendryes and registered, not decided, by the handbooks (LEIA; Koch, s.v. Ogma).

domains.title: The Honey-Tongued Champion
domains.subtitle: Eloquence, Writing
domains.lead: Ogma is the champion — in trenfer, the strong man — of the Túatha Dé Danann, and the Irish tradition made his strength and his speech one gift: the Auraicept na n-Éces calls him a man well skilled in speech and in poetry, and credits him with the invention of the ogham itself. His Gaulish cognate Ogmios, the old-man Herakles of Lucian's account, drags a willing crowd by golden chains fastened to his tongue: in the Celtic world, eloquence is what the strongest god is for.

cards.name: The Ogham
cards.desc: The notched alphabet of early Ireland, carved along the edge of standing stones — of which the Scholars' Primer says: the father of the ogham is Ogma, the mother of the ogham is the hand or knife of Ogma.

cards.name: Orna, the Speaking Sword
cards.desc: The sword of Tethra, king of the Fomorians, found by Ogma after Mag Tuired — which recounted every deed that had been done with it, as swords did in those days.

cards.name: The Flagstone of Tara
cards.desc: The great stone Ogma hurled to test the stranger at the gate — which Lugh threw back through the rath to its own place, proving the stronger champion had arrived.

cards.name: The Firewood
cards.desc: The champion's portion under the tyranny of Bres: hauling fuel for a usurper's fires, so weakened by hunger that the sea washed over him as he carried it.

symbols.name: The ogham fews
symbols.meaning: The notched letters along the stemline — writing itself, fathered by the champion's hand

symbols.name: Orna, Tethra's sword
symbols.meaning: The weapon that tells its own deeds — even the champion's steel answers to speech

symbols.name: The flagstone of Tara
symbols.meaning: Strength as the doorkeeper's test — the stone only the worthiest arm can move

symbols.name: The firewood bundle
symbols.meaning: The strong man reduced to serf-labor — endurance under the usurper, repaid at Mag Tuired

symbols.name: The golden chains of Ogmios
symbols.meaning: Lucian's Gaulish image of eloquence: men led willingly, ear fastened to tongue

mythology.lead: Ogma's dossier is compact and exact: the Lebor Gabála gives his lineage, Cath Maige Tuired gives his deeds — the serf-labor under Bres, the flagstone test at Lugh's coming, the killing of the Fomorian king's son, and the talking sword — and the learned tradition gives him his strangest honor, the invention of the ogham.

myths.title: The Son of Elatha
myths.text: The Lebor Gabála Érenn, Ireland's medieval book of invasions, writes Ogma into the divine genealogy: Ogma son of Elatha, of the line of Delbaeth, and brother of the Dagda himself. When the Túatha Dé Danann came to Ireland out of the four northern cities, Ogma came with them as the champion of the race — in trenfer, the strong man, the standing title the texts give him. His place in the pantheon is therefore double from the first mention: the arm of the Túatha Dé Danann, and the brother of their all-father.

myths.title: The Firewood of the Serf-Years
myths.text: When the half-Fomorian Bres was made king and laid the Túatha Dé Danann under tribute, the greatest of them were put to work like serfs. The Dagda was set to building raths, and Ogma — the champion of the whole divine race — was set to hauling firewood for the fortress. The tale does not spare him: so weakened was he by hunger that the sea washed over him as he carried the fuel. The image is the tradition's sharpest measure of what Bres' kingship cost: the strong man of the gods, bent double under a usurper's fires.

myths.title: The Flagstone Test
myths.text: When Lugh came to Tara before the battle, asking admission by his arts, it fell to Ogma to test the stranger's strength. Ogma hurled the great flagstone of the rath — a stone beyond ordinary lifting — and Lugh answered by hurling it back through the rath to its own place. Ogma then challenged the newcomer to single combat, and Lugh declined: his arts, he said, would be tested soon enough against the Fomorians. The episode is the tradition's own changing of the guard — the old champion making way, stone by stone, for the many-skilled king who would lead the war.

myths.title: Indech Slain, and the Sword That Spoke
myths.text: At the second battle of Mag Tuired the champion earned his title back. In the press of the fighting Ogma killed Indech, son of Dé Domnann, the Fomorian king — the same Indech whose blood the Mórrígan had promised to the Dagda at the ford. And after the battle came the strangest prize in the Irish corpus: among the spoils Ogma found Orna, the sword of Tethra, king of the Fomorians. He unsheathed it and cleaned it, and the sword recounted all the deeds that had been done with it — for it was the custom of swords in those days, when drawn, to tell what they had done. The champion of the gods carried the only weapon in the world that could bear witness to itself.

myths.title: The Recovery of the Harp
myths.text: After the rout, the Fomorians had carried off the Dagda's harper, and the harp itself hung on the wall of the hall where Bres feasted. Three of the Túatha Dé Danann went in pursuit: Lugh, the Dagda, and Ogma — the king, the all-father, and the champion. The Dagda called the harp by its names, and it sprang from the wall to his hand, killing nine men in its path, and played the three strains of weeping, laughter, and sleep until the whole enemy host slept. Ogma walked out of that hall beside his brother and his king, through sleeping foes — the serf of the firewood years restored to the company of the gods' great deeds.

myths.title: The Father of the Ogham
myths.text: The Scholars' Primer — the Auraicept na n-Éces, the medieval Irish grammar of the poets — closes Ogma's dossier with the honor no other Irish god receives. Ogma, a man well skilled in speech and in poetry, invented the ogham for the speaking of Gaelic; and the tract fixes the paternity in a formula: the father of the ogham is Ogma, and the mother of the ogham is the hand or the knife of Ogma. The glossarial tradition adds the epithet Grianainech, the Sun-faced. The champion who hauled firewood under a usurper is the same figure the learned tradition made the author of the alphabet itself — strength and letters, in Ireland, kept in one hand.

lore.syncretism: Ogma has the strongest cross-border witness of any Irish god, and it is a classical author's eyewitness account. Lucian of Samosata, writing in the second century CE, describes a picture the Gauls showed him of their Herakles: not the young Greek athlete but a very old man, bald and wrinkled and sun-dark, drawing after him a great crowd of men — each one fastened by the ears to the god's tongue with slender chains of gold and amber, and following willingly, none struggling. The Gauls, Lucian's guide explains, do not give eloquence to Hermes as the Greeks do; they give it to Herakles, because he is the more powerful, and because the hero achieves everything by persuasion — his arrows are words. In the Gaulish tongue, the guide adds, Herakles is called Ogmios. The equation Ogmios = Ogma is the standard comparison of the handbooks — Vendryes' LEIA derives the Irish name from Proto-Celtic *Ogmios, and Mac Cana and Koch print the Lucian passage as the god's continental portrait. It remains comparison rather than identification: the Irish texts never call Ogma old or bald, and the ogham invention is Ireland's own learned myth. The Welsh corpus, meanwhile, is silent — the Mabinogi knows no counterpart, and no scholar has convincingly supplied one.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ogma's afterlife runs on the two rails his name already laid down: strength and letters. Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) carried Cath Maige Tuired into English and made the champion of the firewood years part of the revival's reading; the later romantic cycle, in Oidheadh Chloinne Tuireann, made him the father of Tuireann and so grandfather of the three sons whose blood-price Lugh exacted. His larger legacy is the script itself. The four hundred ogham stones of Ireland and Wales became the national patrimony of early Ireland, and with them Ogma's paternity: the medieval claim that the champion fathered the alphabet is quoted wherever the stones are studied. In the twentieth century Robert Graves's The White Goddess (1948) built a whole modern mythology on the ogham letters — a construction of Graves's own, not a medieval doctrine — and carried the script, and with it Ogma's fame, into modern esoteric and Druid practice, where he is honored as the god of eloquence, writing, and the poet's craft. The scholars, meanwhile, kept the older wonder alive: Lucian's chained crowd remains the most-quoted image of Celtic eloquence in the literature.
lore.extendedMeditation: Ogma is the Celtic answer to a question every culture asks: what is strength for? The Irish texts could have left him a strong man — the champion who carries the wood, hurls the stone, and kills the Fomorian king's son, and nothing more. Instead the learned tradition took the same hand that dragged the firewood and made it the mother of the alphabet, and the Gauls, three centuries before the Irish manuscripts, had already painted the answer: the strongest god is the one whose victories need no chains, because men follow his tongue willingly. Even Ogma's weapon obeys the rule — Orna, the sword of the enemy king, becomes precious not for what it cut but for what it tells. The champion's whole dossier argues one proposition: the word is the deed that survives the doing. The stones of Ireland still stand along their stemlines, notched with the letters Ireland assigned to Ogma's paternity — the strongest kind of monument, because it is made of speech.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Ogma — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script of the great codices; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham — the very script the medieval tradition credits Ogma with inventing — survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: ogma.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Ogma is a textual god: no ogham stone names him, no votive inscription invokes him, and the irony is the corpus's own — the script the medieval scholars fathered on him survives on some four hundred stones of roughly the fourth to seventh centuries, bearing personal names in formulaic genitives, none of them his. His manuscript witnesses are exact: Cath Maige Tuired survives uniquely in the sixteenth-century British Library MS Harley 5280, the basis of Gray's edition; the Lebor Gabála Érenn is preserved in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster and its sister codices; and the Auraicept na n-Éces, the tract that credits him with the alphabet, comes down in the great late-medieval compilations such as the Book of Ballymote. The nearest material witness to his figure is classical rather than Celtic: Lucian's second-century description of the Gaulish Ogmios, the old Herakles of eloquence, is the continental portrait of the god, and the Gaulish name is otherwise attested on a small number of defixiones (curse tablets) — comparative evidence, never identification.
